title: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
summary: How serving engines keep KV blocks in CPU DRAM, SSD and remote stores, when loading them beats re-running prefill, how layer-wise loading hides transfers, and how tiers choose what to evict.
outcomes: Explain why the GPU prefix cache runs out and what each offload tier (HBM, DRAM, SSD, remote) adds
Compute load time vs prefill time for a model, prompt length, link bandwidth and GPU throughput
Estimate TTFT with layer-wise loading and explain when overlap helps
Trace how a request's prefix is matched across tiers and why only a contiguous prefix counts
Choose admission and eviction policies for multi-turn and shared-prefix workloads

lessons.title: Why the GPU prefix cache runs out, and where KV can go

blocks.md: From the PagedAttention course you know that vLLM keeps KV in fixed-size blocks and reuses a cached prefix by hashing full blocks. That reuse has one hard limit: the blocks must still be in **GPU high-bandwidth memory (HBM)**. When HBM fills, the least valuable blocks are evicted and their KV is gone. The next request that needs them pays for a full prefill again.

Workloads that reuse long contexts hit this limit fast. The CachedAttention paper (USENIX ATC 2024) found that 73% of ShareGPT conversations are multi-turn, and that recomputing the history can be up to 99% of prefill cost in later turns. It also estimated that free HBM on its 4 x A100 server would fill with KV in about 14 seconds of serving. Agents, RAG over the same documents and long system prompts show the same pattern: the same prefix comes back, but minutes later, long after HBM evicted it.

**KV cache offloading** keeps evicted (or copied) KV blocks in slower but much larger memory: CPU DRAM, local NVMe SSD, or a remote store shared by many servers. A later hit loads those bytes back instead of running prefill again. Let's size the problem with a concrete model: **Llama 3 8B** in BF16 has 32 layers, 8 KV heads and head size 128, so every token stores $2 \times 32 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 131{,}072$ bytes (128 KiB) of K and V.

blocks.title: How many 8K-token prompts of Llama 3 8B KV fit per tier

scenes.caption: At 128 KiB of KV per token, one 8,192-token prompt needs 1 GiB. 40 GB of free HBM holds 37 such prompts; 512 GB of host DRAM holds 476.
A 4 TB SSD holds 3,725. Capacities are assumed round numbers for one server; the point is the gap: about 13x more from HBM to DRAM and 100x to SSD.

blocks.title: The KV tier hierarchy and the paths between tiers

scenes.caption: Four tiers, fastest and smallest first. Names differ by system: Dynamo's KV Block Manager calls them G1 to G4, SGLang HiCache calls GPU, host and storage L1, L2 and L3. LMCache instead calls CPU memory L1.
Store path: when a KV block is complete, a copy goes to pinned host memory with an asynchronous DMA (cudaMemcpyAsync in vLLM), overlapping model compute. The GPU copy stays until GPU eviction.
Lower tiers are fed from host memory. In vLLM's tiered spec, secondary tiers (filesystem, object store, peer instances) cannot touch GPU memory, so everything is staged through the CPU tier.
Hit path: a later request whose prefix lives in a lower tier has those blocks promoted back up, through host memory, into GPU blocks, instead of recomputing them with prefill.

Some managers skip the hop: Dynamo's KVBM can onboard a disk block straight into GPU memory through NIXL (NVIDIA's data-transfer library), possibly using GPUDirect Storage. The tiers are the same; only the data path changes.

blocks.md: Two different reasons to offload exist, and this course is about the first. **Reuse offloading** (LMCache, vLLM's OffloadingConnector, SGLang HiCache, Mooncake, Dynamo KVBM) saves KV so a *future request* can skip prefill. **Capacity offloading** (FlexGen, InfiniGen) keeps the KV of the *current* batch partly in CPU memory during decoding so a bigger batch or longer context fits; FlexGen ran OPT-175B on a single 16 GB GPU this way, and InfiniGen prefetches only the KV entries it predicts the next layer will attend to strongly.

Offloading does not make attention read from CPU memory. In reuse offloading, blocks are copied back into GPU blocks before the attention kernel runs; the kernel only ever sees HBM. What offloading buys is skipping the *prefill compute* that would otherwise recreate those blocks.
Each tier down is roughly 10x bigger and slower. Offloading turns a prefix-cache miss into a load from a lower tier, which pays off only if the load is faster than recomputing.

blocks.question: A server runs Llama 3 8B with 40 GB of HBM free for KV and serves 200 users who each come back every few minutes with a growing 8K-token chat history. Without offloading, what happens on most return visits?
options: Prefix caching hits, because vLLM never evicts blocks that another request might reuse
The history was evicted from HBM (only about 37 such histories fit), so prefill recomputes it
The attention kernel reads the history directly from CPU memory over PCIe
The request is rejected until enough HBM is freed
blocks.explain: 200 histories of 1 GiB each cannot fit in 40 GB; only about 37 can. Free blocks are evicted when space is needed, so most returning users miss and pay a full prefill. Offloading to a 512 GB DRAM tier would keep all 200 histories.

blocks.question: Which system is an example of capacity offloading rather than reuse offloading?
options: LMCache storing chunks in Redis for other engines
SGLang HiCache writing radix-tree nodes to host memory
FlexGen placing part of the attention cache in CPU memory during decoding
vLLM's OffloadingConnector copying finished prompt blocks to pinned memory
blocks.explain: FlexGen offloads weights, activations and KV of the running batch to fit a huge model on a small GPU and maximize throughput. The other three save KV so later requests that share the prefix can skip prefill.

lessons.title: Reload or recompute: bytes versus prefill FLOPs

blocks.md: A cache hit in a lower tier is not automatically a win. You can get the KV for a prefix in two ways: **recompute** it by running prefill on the GPU, or **load** the saved bytes over some link. The faster option wins, so we need a cost model for each. We will use Llama 3 8B, BF16, and *stated assumptions* for hardware: the GPU sustains 400 TFLOPS on prefill, and each tier has an effective bandwidth (host DRAM over PCIe 50 GB/s, a remote RDMA pool 12 GB/s, local NVMe 6 GB/s, an object store 1 GB/s). These are round planning numbers, not measurements.

blocks.tex: b_{kv} = 2 \cdot L \cdot h_{kv} \cdot d_h \cdot s = 2 \cdot 32 \cdot 8 \cdot 128 \cdot 2 = 131{,}072 \text{ bytes}, \qquad T_{load}(n) = \frac{n\, b_{kv}}{B}
blocks.caption: Bytes per token: K and V, for L layers, h_kv KV heads of size d_h, s bytes per value. Load time is linear in the prompt length n.

blocks.tex: T_{rec}(n) \approx \frac{2 P n + 2 L d\, n^2}{F}
blocks.caption: Prefill FLOPs: 2 FLOPs per weight per token (P = 6.98e9 weights in the linear layers of Llama 3 8B), plus causal attention (QK and AV) with d = 4096 query dimensions per layer. F is GPU throughput.

blocks.md: The ratio is what matters. Per token, short-prompt prefill costs about $2P = 14$ GFLOPs while the KV is only 131 KB, roughly 100,000 FLOPs per byte. Setting $T_{load} = T_{rec}$ gives the **break-even bandwidth** $B^* = n\, b_{kv} F / \text{FLOPs}(n)$: any tier faster than $B^*$ should be read rather than recomputed. For Llama 3 8B at 400 TFLOPS, $B^*$ is 3.7 GB/s at 1K tokens and 3.3 GB/s at 8K.

scenes.caption: Prefill of 8,192 tokens costs 1.32e14 FLOPs; at an assumed 400 TFLOPS that is 330 ms. The KV it produces is 1.07 GB.
Loading the same 1.07 GB at assumed effective bandwidths: 21.5 ms from host DRAM at 50 GB/s, 89.5 ms from a remote pool at 12 GB/s, 179 ms from NVMe at 6 GB/s. All beat prefill.
An object store at 1 GB/s needs 1,074 ms, over 3x slower than recomputing. A tier is only worth reading when its bandwidth beats the break-even point, here 3.3 GB/s.

blocks.title: Recompute vs load time as the prompt grows (Llama 3 8B)

scenes.caption: Host DRAM at 50 GB/s: loading is 13x to 79x faster than prefill at every length shown. Both curves rise, but prefill bends upward because attention cost grows with the square of the length.
NVMe at 6 GB/s: still faster than recomputing everywhere (1.6x at 1K tokens, 2.6x at 32K), but the gap is now small.
An object store at 1 GB/s: loading loses until prompts reach about 147K tokens, where quadratic attention finally makes prefill slower than a linear byte copy.
A faster GPU moves the line. At 1,000 TFLOPS, NVMe at 6 GB/s loses to recompute below about 30K tokens; break-even bandwidth rises to 8 to 9 GB/s.

blocks.prompt: Llama 3 70B has 80 layers and also 8 KV heads. Compared with the 8B model, does it need a faster or a slower link before loading beats recomputing?
blocks.reveal: **Slower.** Its KV is $2 \times 80 \times 8 \times 128 \times 2 = 327{,}680$ bytes per token, only 2.5x the 8B model, because grouped-query attention keeps just 8 KV heads. But its linear layers have 6.85e10 weights, about 10x more FLOPs per token. Break-even bandwidth at 8K tokens drops from 3.26 GB/s to 0.89 GB/s. Bigger GQA models are *easier* to offload profitably.

blocks.md: The 400 TFLOPS assumes the GPU is otherwise idle. On a busy server, recomputing a prefix steals compute from every other request in the batch, while a load mostly uses the copy engine and the PCIe or network link. So loading can win even when the TTFT numbers look tied. The reverse also happens: the LMCache paper reports that with a 15 Gbps remote store, loading can take longer than prefill for short contexts or small models.

You can also do both. **Cake** (Jin et al., 2024) splits one prefix between the two resources: the GPU computes KV chunks forward from token 0 while an I/O thread loads chunks backward from the end, and they stop where they meet. Later tokens are the expensive ones to compute (they attend to everything before them) but cost the same to load, so loading from the back is the right split. vLLM exposes a simpler knob, `max_load_tokens` (experimental, per request), which caps how many tokens are loaded from offloaded storage; tokens beyond the cap are recomputed.

Compare bytes over bandwidth with FLOPs over throughput. Fast tiers (host DRAM, RDMA pools) beat prefill at almost any length; slow tiers only pay off for long prompts, big models, or a GPU that is busy anyway.

blocks.question: Your NVMe tier delivers 6 GB/s. You upgrade the GPU from 400 to 1,000 effective TFLOPS and keep serving Llama 3 8B with 8K-token prompts. What happens to the case for reading KV from NVMe?
options: It gets stronger: a faster GPU also transfers data faster
Nothing changes: the decision depends only on prompt length
It weakens: recompute drops to 132 ms, while the 179 ms NVMe load stays the same, so recomputing now wins
It weakens only for prompts longer than 32K tokens
blocks.explain: Load time depends on bytes and link bandwidth, not on GPU FLOPs. Prefill time falls from 330 ms to 132 ms with the faster GPU, so the 179 ms NVMe read now loses at 8K tokens. Break-even bandwidth rises to about 8 GB/s, and NVMe only wins above roughly 30K tokens.

blocks.question: A colleague says: 'Prefill cost grows faster than load cost as prompts get longer, so offloading pays off more for long prompts.' Which part of the cost model makes this true?
options: KV bytes per token grow with prompt length
The attention term in prefill grows with $n^2$ while bytes grow with $n$
Longer prompts compress better on disk
PCIe bandwidth increases for larger transfers
blocks.explain: Every token stores the same 131,072 bytes, so load time is linear in $n$. Prefill has the linear-layer term $2Pn$ plus causal attention $2Ldn^2$, which dominates at long lengths. That is why even a 1 GB/s object store beats prefill beyond about 147K tokens in this model.

lessons.title: Hiding the transfer: layer-wise loading and asynchronous saving

blocks.md: A transformer computes one layer at a time, and layer $i$ only needs layer $i$'s KV. So nothing forces us to wait for the whole cache before starting. **Layer-wise loading** uses two CUDA streams: a copy stream brings layer $i+1$'s KV into HBM while the compute stream runs layer $i$. CachedAttention calls this layer-wise pre-loading, SGLang HiCache loads layer N+1 while computing layer N, and LMCache gives each layer separate compute and data-movement streams with a buffer that holds only one layer's KV.

blocks.title: Layer-wise loading on a toy 4-layer model

scenes.caption: Naive: load all 4 layers of cached KV (3 ms each), then compute the new tokens layer by layer (2 ms each). The first token waits for the sum: 20 ms.
Layer-wise: layer 0 can start as soon as its own KV has arrived. Compute of layer i overlaps the load of layer i+1. Done at 14 ms: the total load (12) plus one layer of compute (2).
If compute dominates (1 ms load, 3 ms compute per layer), loading hides almost completely: 13 ms is the 12 ms of compute plus one layer of load.
Load-bound again, but a previous job holds the GPU until 6 ms and loading only starts when this job starts. Finish: 20 ms.
CachedAttention's fix: a reserved HBM read buffer lets the first layers preload while the previous job still runs. Here two layers preload during 0 to 6 ms and the job finishes at 14 ms.

blocks.caption: Simplified model with L identical layers: the slower stream sets the pace, and only one layer of the faster stream is left exposed at the start or end.

blocks.md: Now a real-sized example: the second turn of a chat on Llama 3 8B. The first turn left 8,192 tokens of KV (1.07 GB) in host DRAM, and the user adds 512 new tokens. The new tokens cost 9.41e12 FLOPs (they also attend over the 8,192 cached keys), which is 23.5 ms at 400 TFLOPS.

blocks.title: Turn 2 of a chat: 8,192 cached tokens plus 512 new (Llama 3 8B)

scenes.caption: Without any cache, prefill must process all 8,704 tokens: 353 ms at 400 TFLOPS.
With the history in host DRAM: the 1.07 GB load takes 21.5 ms and the 512 new tokens take 23.5 ms. Run back to back that is 45.0 ms; overlapped layer by layer it is 24.2 ms.
From NVMe at 6 GB/s the load (179 ms) dominates, so overlap only hides the small compute: 202.5 ms sequential vs 179.7 ms layer-wise. Still about 2x better than recomputing.

blocks.prompt: In the NVMe case, layer-wise loading saved only 23 ms out of 202 ms. What would make overlap save more?
blocks.reveal: Overlap can hide at most the *smaller* of the two streams. With 179 ms of load and 23.5 ms of compute, compute is all there is to hide. Overlap helps most when the two are balanced, as in the host DRAM case (21.5 vs 23.5 ms), where it nearly halves TTFT. To speed up the NVMe case you must cut bytes (a faster tier, prefetching to DRAM ahead of time, or KV compression) rather than overlap more.

blocks.md: CachedAttention states the same condition for when overlap is not enough: if the per-token load time times the history length exceeds the per-token prefill time times the new length, loading is exposed. It reserves an HBM **read buffer** so pre-loading can start while the previous job is still on the GPU. In its ablation (LLaMA-13B, 1K history tokens, 100 new tokens), layer-wise pre-loading without the buffer cut prefill time by 35%, and with a 15-layer buffer by 61%.

Saving runs the other way. **Asynchronous saving** writes KV out to host memory layer by layer while the GPU keeps working, using an HBM write buffer so the next job is not blocked; CachedAttention reports 13% to 15% lower execution time from it. vLLM's OffloadingConnector copies completed blocks into pinned host memory with `cudaMemcpyAsync` as they are produced, and Dynamo's KVBM performs its offloads and onboards asynchronously at the end of the forward pass.

Pinned (page-locked) host memory matters. Asynchronous DMA copies need it; vLLM reserves `cpu_bytes_to_use` bytes of pinned host memory for its CPU tier, and Dynamo's G2 host pool is pinned memory, rather than ordinary pageable buffers.
Overlap turns load plus compute into roughly max(load, compute). It is free speed when the two are balanced and nearly useless when one dominates.

blocks.question: A deployment loads a 2 GB cached prefix at 25 GB/s (80 ms) and computes the new tokens in 10 ms over 40 layers. Using the simplified overlap model, what TTFT should layer-wise loading give?
options: About 90 ms, because overlap cannot help a load-bound case
About 80 ms: the load dominates and only one layer of compute (0.25 ms) is exposed
About 45 ms, because the two streams split the work
About 10 ms, because the load is hidden behind compute
blocks.explain: max(80, 10) + min(80, 10)/40 = 80 + 0.25 ms. All compute hides under the load, but the load itself cannot hide behind anything. Sequential would be 90 ms, so overlap saves the 10 ms of compute and no more.

blocks.question: Why can layer-wise loading start computing layer 0 before layers 1 to 31 of the cached KV have arrived?
options: Because attention at layer 0 only reads layer 0's keys and values
Because the GPU recomputes the missing layers in parallel
Because KV caches are stored layer-interleaved by token
Because the scheduler skips attention for cached tokens
blocks.explain: Each layer's attention uses only the K and V produced at that same layer. Layer 0 needs nothing from deeper layers, so it can run as soon as its own KV is in HBM while later layers are still in flight.

lessons.title: Finding a prefix across tiers, requests and engines

blocks.md: Offload tiers reuse the same key the GPU prefix cache uses: a hash of a block's tokens chained with the hash of everything before it. That makes a stored chunk meaningful to *any* request with the same prefix, whether it comes from the same user later, another user sharing a system prompt, or another engine instance reading a shared store. Granularity varies: vLLM's offloaded `block_size` must be a multiple of the GPU block size, and LMCache stores KV in chunks of 256 tokens by default.

Because keys are chained, only a **contiguous prefix** counts. The lookup walks the request's blocks in order, first in HBM, then in the offload tiers, and stops at the first block found nowhere. The code below is a simplified planner in that spirit (real connectors work in tokens, align to block boundaries and batch the lookups).

blocks.title: Planning a request across tiers (simplified)

scenes.caption: An 8-block prompt arrives. Each block is identified by a chained hash of its tokens and all earlier tokens, so h5 can only be valid if h0 to h4 are the same prefix.
First, the ordinary GPU prefix cache: h0 and h1 are in HBM, h2 is not. Two blocks need no transfer at all.
Next, the offload tiers, still walking the prefix in order. h2, h3, h4 come from the CPU tier, h5 only exists in the remote store.
h6 is nowhere, so the walk stops. h7 is sitting in the CPU tier but cannot be used: its KV was computed after a prefix that included h6, and that position must be recomputed first.
Result: 2 GPU hits, 4 loads, 2 blocks of prefill. A cap like vLLM's max_load_tokens would truncate the load list here and push the rest into prefill.

blocks.md: A cached block after a gap is useless for this request. KV at position 7 depends on every earlier token through attention in every layer, so if block 6 must be recomputed, block 7 must be too, even if an identical hash for it were stored. Eviction that removes a middle block silently strands everything after it.

Once the plan is made, transfers are scheduled so the GPU keeps working. SGLang's HiCache shows the whole flow with three tiers: L1 is GPU memory, L2 is host memory private to the instance, and L3 is distributed storage that can be shared across instances (backends include file, Mooncake, 3FS, NIXL and AIBrix).

blocks.title: SGLang HiCache: a request with hits in all three tiers

scenes.caption: Local match first: the HiRadixTree records which tokens sit in L1 and L2, and returns a prefix whose first part is in GPU memory and the rest in host memory.
The tree keeps no L3 metadata, so the scheduler asks the storage backend in real time how much more of the prefix it holds.
If the L3 hit exceeds a threshold (256 tokens by default), a prefetch copies those pages from L3 into local host memory.
The prefetch policy decides how long to wait: best_effort stops as soon as the GPU can run prefill, wait_complete waits for everything, timeout waits up to a limit that grows with hit length.
Everything now local is loaded into GPU memory, overlapping layer N+1's copy with layer N's compute, and prefill runs only on the tokens nobody had.

blocks.md: Sharing across machines is where the remote tier earns its keep. **Mooncake**, the serving platform for Moonshot AI's Kimi, builds a disaggregated KV cache out of the otherwise underused CPU DRAM and SSD of the GPU cluster. Its Mooncake Store keeps multiple replicas of hot objects to spread read load and moves data with its Transfer Engine using GPUDirect RDMA across multiple NICs. The same connector interfaces (LMCache, NIXL, Mooncake) also ship KV from a prefill worker to a decode worker in disaggregated serving: offloading and P/D transfer are the same mechanism with a different reader.
Offload tiers are a bigger prefix cache with the same keys. A hit is the longest contiguous prefix found across all tiers; everything after the first gap is prefill.

blocks.question: A request's blocks are h0 to h9. HBM holds h0 to h3. The CPU tier holds h0 to h6 and h8, h9. What gets loaded from CPU, and what is recomputed?
options: Load h4 to h6 and h8, h9; recompute h7
Load h4 to h6; recompute h7, h8, h9
Load nothing; recompute h4 to h9, since the CPU tier has a gap
Load h0 to h6 again from CPU to refresh them; recompute h7 to h9
blocks.explain: The usable prefix stops at the first block that is nowhere: h7. h4 to h6 extend the GPU hit contiguously, so they are loaded. h8 and h9 were computed after a context that includes h7, which must be recomputed, so they are recomputed along with it.

blocks.question: In SGLang HiCache with the best_effort prefetch policy, a 4,000-token L3 hit is only half fetched when the GPU becomes free. What happens?
options: The fetched part is used with the local hits and the rest is computed by prefill
The request waits until all 4,000 tokens arrive
The partial prefetch is discarded and everything is recomputed
The request is moved to another instance that has the data in L2
blocks.explain: best_effort terminates prefetching as soon as the GPU can run prefill. The data already fetched is used together with the local data, and the remaining tokens are prefilled. wait_complete would have waited for all of it.

lessons.title: Eviction and placement: what stays, what sinks, what is dropped

blocks.md: Every tier is finite, so each one needs an **admission** rule (what gets written in) and an **eviction** rule (what leaves when it is full). Evicting from HBM can mean demoting to host memory; evicting from the bottom tier means the KV is gone and the next request recomputes it.

Most systems default to recency. vLLM's OffloadingConnector takes `eviction_policy` of `lru` (the default) or `arc`; ARC (adaptive replacement cache) keeps a recency list and a frequency list and adapts how much space each gets. LMCache's multiprocess mode offers LRU, ARC and IsolatedLRU, evicting 20% of allocated memory per cycle once usage passes an 80% watermark. Mooncake Store uses approximate LRU: at 90% usage it evicts 5% of objects, and it skips any object under a **lease** (granted for 10 seconds by default when a client looks it up) so a block is not freed while a client that just looked it up reads it (if the lease expires mid-read, the read fails rather than return freed data).

Admission matters as much. vLLM's `offload_prompt_only` (on by default) offloads prompt blocks and skips decode blocks, and `store_threshold` can require a minimum number of lookups before a block is offloaded. SGLang HiCache chooses among `write_through` (every access is written to the next level), `write_through_selective` (only after access frequency passes a threshold) and `write_back` (written down only when evicted from the level above).

blocks.title: A 3-session host tier: LRU vs queue-aware eviction

scenes.caption: Three sessions fill the 3-slot host tier (a miss means fetching from SSD or recomputing). Both policies agree so far.
Session A returns: a hit for both.
D arrives. LRU evicts B, the least recently used. Look-ahead sees B coming back soon in the queue and evicts C, whose next use is farthest away.
B returns: a miss for LRU, which just threw it away; a hit for look-ahead.
E is a one-off session. LRU evicts A to make room; look-ahead evicts D, which is not needed until much later.
A returns: LRU misses again. Look-ahead hits. Recency is a poor signal when sessions return in a cycle longer than the cache.
B returns. LRU evicted it again at the previous request (C took its slot); look-ahead kept it.
After 12 requests: LRU 1 hit, look-ahead 5 hits on the same capacity. Simplified: this look-ahead knows the whole future; a real scheduler only sees its queue.

blocks.md: The toy shows why recency fails for multi-turn chat: sessions return in a cycle longer than the cache, so LRU evicts exactly what comes back next. CachedAttention exploits the fact that the serving scheduler *knows* which jobs are queued. It prefetches the KV of waiting jobs from disk to host memory within a look-ahead window, protects sessions inside a look-ahead eviction window, and evicts at the granularity of a whole session, since a conversation's KV is used all together or not at all.

blocks.title: Hit rates reported by CachedAttention (128 GB DRAM, 10 TB SSD)

scenes.caption: With the same hardware, scheduler-aware placement reached an 86% hit rate versus 58% for LRU and 48% for FIFO in the paper's multi-turn evaluation.

blocks.md: Do not evict a prefix's parent before its children. Because keys are chained, removing an early block makes every later block of that prefix unreachable, yet those stranded blocks still occupy space. SGLang's radix tree evicts leaves first for this reason, and Mooncake Store can evict a group of related objects (such as the separate K and V tensors of one entry) all or none.

Failure modes to watch for in production: the PCIe or network link is shared with other traffic, so measured load bandwidth can be far below the planning number; pinned host memory is reserved up front and competes with everything else on the host; cache keys must include anything that changes the KV (model, weights version, dtype, LoRA adapter), or a hit returns wrong values; and a remote tier adds tail latency, which is why HiCache bounds prefetch waits and vLLM can cap loads per request.

Choose eviction by reuse pattern, not habit. LRU is a fine default; workloads with known future reuse (queued multi-turn sessions, scheduled agent steps) do much better with placement driven by the scheduler.

blocks.question: A chatbot has 1,000 active sessions that each return every 5 minutes, and the host tier holds 600 sessions. Under strict LRU, what hit rate should you expect for returning sessions, and why?
options: About 60%, because the tier holds 60% of sessions
100%, because LRU keeps recently active sessions
About 50%, because LRU and FIFO behave the same here
Close to 0%, because each session is the least recently used by the time it returns, so it was just evicted
blocks.explain: With a cyclic access pattern larger than the cache, LRU evicts the oldest session, which is exactly the next one to return. Every return misses. Admission filtering that keeps a fixed subset resident, a bigger tier (SSD) or scheduler look-ahead all fix this; matching capacity alone does not.

blocks.question: An engineer configures an offload store whose keys are the hash of the token IDs only. They then deploy a new fine-tuned version of the model behind the same store. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: KV depends only on the tokens
Every lookup misses because the hashes change
Hits return KV computed by the old weights, silently corrupting outputs
The store evicts all old entries automatically on deploy
blocks.explain: K and V are projections of hidden states through the model's weights, so different weights give different KV for the same tokens. Keys must include the model identity (and dtype, adapter, and similar), or stale KV is served as a hit.
